newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Iran urge Afghan groups to hold peace talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Iran urge Afghan groups to hold peace talks.

text.p: India and Iran urged warring factions on Thursday to end the civil war in Afghanistan and called on its neighbouring countries to use their influence to win a peaceful solution.

Indian Minister of External Affairs Inder Gujral told Reuters at the end of two hours of talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati that both countries wanted an end to "outside involvement" in the latest upsurge of fighting.
"The problem of Afghanistan should be left to the Afghan people," Gujral said. "All parties in Afghanistan should get together and should solve the problems of Afghanistan peacefully."

The Iranian minister arrived on Thursday after a lightning tour of the former Soviet republics of Central Asia to discuss Afghanistan, where government forces are battling Islamic Taleban militia who drove them out of the capital last month.
Velayati told reporters after his talks with Gujral that any foreign intervention would worsen the crisis there.

"There is no military solution for Afghanistan," he said. "Any kind of foreign intervention in Afghanistan will deteriorate the situation. Iran and India are against any foreign intervention in the internal affairs of Afghanistan."
Gujral declined to name countries he believed were involved, but said: "Both of us have our assessments of who are involved."
India had close ties with former Soviet-backed communist rulers of Afghanistan but Gujral hinted that communist rule had contributed to the increased suffering of Afghans.
"The people of Afghanistan have suffered immensely in the last two decades," he said. "It is high time they were relieved of the stranglehold of misery."
Velayati went into a meeting with Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda before returning to Tehran later on Thursday.
Asked if there was a realistic chance of an early end to the war, Gujral said: "If all the neighbouring countries exert their influence in the right direction, it may end soon."
Pakistan has offered to mediate between warring factions.

Indian officials said that offer was unlikely to suit Iran or India, where the media have accused Pakistan, the United States and Saudi Arabia of provoking a crisis inside Afghanistan, a country torn by years of civil war.
Iran and India recognise the government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, driven out of the Afghan capital last month.
Velayati's visit precedes one by Indian Vice President Kocheril Raman Narayanan to Iran from October 22.
